title: Two-colour brioche throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw in two-colour brioche on 5.5 mm needles.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw in DK on 5.5 mm needles, worked in two-colour brioche: Colour A on RS rows, Colour B on WS rows. The RS and WS are mirror-image colour inversions. ADVANCED: two-colour brioche requires tracking two sets of row types simultaneously and managing two active yarns on every pass.
sourceNotes: Two-colour brioche is documented in Barbara Walker, A Treasury of Knitting Patterns (1968), §Two-Colour Brioche, as an advanced technique producing a reversible colour-inversion fabric. The brk/brp abbreviations and two-colour setup are also described in Weldon's Practical Knitter, 9th series (1893), §Colour Brioche Work.

knitting.gaugeText: 15 sts × 26 brioche row-pairs = 10 × 10 cm in two-colour brioche on 5.5 mm needles, unblocked. Each brioche pass counts as half a row.

stitchCountCheckpoints.label: Halfway check — 150 working sts, about 60 cm (312 passes total at midpoint)

glossaryTerms.definition: A brioche knitting technique where two yarn colours are alternated every pass. On RS passes, Colour A works the brk stitches while Colour B stitches are slipped. On WS passes, Colour B works its stitches while Colour A stitches are slipped. The RS and WS show opposite colour arrangements — what appears dark on the RS appears light on the WS, and vice versa.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat on 5.5 mm needles in
two-colour brioche
, finishing at 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

Single-panel construction; no seaming. This throw is rated ADVANCED because two-colour brioche requires managing two active yarns simultaneously and tracking four distinct row types (RS Colour A, RS Colour B slip pass, WS Colour B, WS Colour A slip pass) in a fixed sequence. The reward is a reversible throw where the RS shows Colour A raised against a recessed Colour B background, while the WS shows the inversion: Colour B raised against Colour A. Budget about 450 g of each colour (about 990 m / 1,083 yards each) of DK. The larger 5.5 mm needle compensates for the doubled structure.
What you need

items.name: Colour A
items.qty: 450 g (about 990 m / 1,083 yards) of DK in a strong or dark colour

items.name: Colour B
items.qty: 450 g of DK in a contrasting or lighter colour

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 5.5 mm (UK 5 / US 9) circular needle, 120 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

15 stitches and 26 row-pairs to 10 cm in two-colour brioche on 5.5 mm needles, unblocked. Two-colour brioche gauge is very different from stocking stitch. Swatch 30 stitches × 50 passes (25 row-pairs) and measure the centre 10 cm × 10 cm after the swatch has relaxed for 30 minutes off the needles.
At 15 stitches per 10 cm, 100 cm requires 150 stitches (a multiple of 2). At 14 per 10 cm, use 140 stitches.
Stitches used

items.name: brk
items.qty: brioche knit: k the slipped stitch and its yo together

items.name: brp
items.qty: brioche purl: p the slipped stitch and its yo together

items.name: A pass / B pass
items.qty: the pass of the needle using the specified colour

content.text: Pattern
Cast-on
Using Colour A and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 150 stitches. Long-tail tail: (5.5 × 150) / 10 + 15 = 82.5 + 15 = 97.5 cm. Measure 115 cm.
Setup row
Using Colour A, work a setup row: *k1, sl1yo; repeat from * to end. This establishes the initial slip-yo pairs for Colour B stitches.
Body (4-pass repeat)
Pass 1 (RS, Colour A): *brk, sl1yo; repeat from * to end. [brk works the Colour A brioche knit stitches; sl1yo slips the Colour B stitches with a yo]
Pass 2 (RS, Colour B): *sl1yo, brk; repeat from * to end. [sl1yo slips the Colour A stitches; brk works the Colour B stitches]
Pass 3 (WS, Colour A): *brp, sl1yo; repeat from * to end.
Pass 4 (WS, Colour B): *sl1yo, brp; repeat from * to end.

Repeat passes 1 to 4 until the throw measures 120 cm. Always begin a new row from the RS with Colour A first. When you set this aside, note which pass number (1, 4) is next and which colour is at the needle tip.
Stitch count check-ins

At pass 312 total (156 row-pairs, about 60 cm): count the working stitches (not counting yo loops). You should have 150 stitches. At pass 624 (about 119 cm): count again. Two-colour brioche is complex; a stitch-count drift is usually caused by a missed brk leaving an extra sl1yo on the needle.
Common faults

Both colours appearing on the same face: pass 1 and pass 2 were worked consecutively in the wrong direction. RS passes must always be worked from right to left (RS facing); WS passes from left to right (WS facing). Do not turn after every pass; two passes of the same direction type are worked before turning.

Yarn tangling at the edge: two yarns are carried up the same edge. Use yarn on one side for Colour A and carry it along that edge; use Colour B on the other side. Alternatively, use two yarn balls positioned on opposite sides of the work.
Cast-off
Work a two-colour brioche cast-off or use a standard cast-off with needles two sizes larger to match the elasticity of the fabric. Cut both yarns and weave in ends.
Finishing
Weave in all four ends (Colour A and B at cast-on and cast-off). The fabric is reversible; no blocking is needed to make it lie flat.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry. Two-colour brioche fabric springs back to its relaxed width after each wash.
What to try next
From two-colour brioche in a 1×1 arrangement, try a 2×2 structure next: brioche knit two, brioche purl two. The columns are bolder. The colour inversion between RS and WS is more dramatic.
